introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (4 questions en tout, au moins 1 par section). `regles_choix` ne sait exprimer que « n parmi m » : chaque section (A, B, C, 4 questions chacune) porte la règle minimale (1 sur 4) ; la règle « 4 en tout » n'est pas exprimable et figure dans `introduction_markdown`.
Points : chaque question imprime « (25 marks) » et le sujet dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` vaut donc 25 pour chaque question. Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les 12 questions) : filigrane et publicités gcerevision.com sans conséquence sur la lisibilité ; aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible. Page de garde vérifiée : « JUNE 2020 », ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, trois heures.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Question à plus haut risque d'imprécision : la « crise du KNDP » (années 1960) est décrite en termes généraux et prudents (rivalité Foncha / dirigeants du gouvernement de l'Ouest, pression d'Ahidjo pour le parti unique, naissance de l'UNC en 1966). Succession des Premiers ministres de l'Ouest-Cameroun (Foncha jusqu'en 1965, Jua 1965-1968, Muna 1968-1972) et passage de la vice-présidence fédérale à Muna en 1970 cités de mémoire. Le sujet ne précise pas la période exacte de la crise : à vérifier avec un manuel du programme avant publication.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Account for and examine the effects of the KNDP Crisis on the State of West Cameroon.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP), founded by John Ngu Foncha in 1955, won the 1959 elections in Southern Cameroons and governed West Cameroon after reunification in 1961, with Foncha as Prime Minister of West Cameroon and Vice-President of the Federal Republic. In the middle of the 1960s the party went through a serious crisis of leadership and direction, the **KNDP crisis**, which divided the party and its government and which took place while the federal President, Ahmadou Ahidjo, was pressing for a single national party. This essay accounts for the crisis and examines its effects on the **State of West Cameroon**. (The sequence of events is given here in broad terms, following the generally accepted outline of the period; the details of the quarrels between individual leaders are not given with more precision than the sources allow.)

**1. Causes of the crisis**

- **Separation of party leadership and government.** After 1961 Foncha, who was both party leader and Vice-President of the Federation, was often at the federal capital, and in 1965 the post of Prime Minister of West Cameroon passed to Augustine Ngom Jua. The authority of the party leader and that of the head of the government were not clearly distinguished, and this produced friction.
- **Leadership rivalry and personal ambition.** Rivalries between Foncha and leading politicians in his own party and cabinet (Jua and, later, S. T. Muna are the names usually mentioned) about leadership, appointments and influence weakened its unity. Many members of the party were also dissatisfied with the way the party was run.
- **Disagreements about policy and about the party's future.** There were differences about relations with the federal government, about the pace of integration with East Cameroon and about whether the KNDP should keep its separate identity or merge with its rival, the Cameroons People's National Convention (CPNC), and the other parties in a larger national party.
- **Pressure from President Ahidjo.** Ahidjo wanted to unify political life under his control. He encouraged the merging of parties and used the quarrels among the Anglophone leaders to strengthen his position. The crisis arose partly from the question of whether West Cameroon's parties should give up their independence and join the new national party.
- **Structural weakness of West Cameroon.** West Cameroon had a small population, limited resources and a dependence on federal decisions and funds, and this gave factions an incentive to seek the support of Yaounde.

**2. Effects on the State of West Cameroon**

- **Political instability and weakened government.** The infighting divided the leadership, distracted the government from administration and development, and reduced the prestige and authority of West Cameroon's Prime Minister and cabinet.
- **Decline of Foncha and of the KNDP.** Foncha lost his control over the party and the government of West Cameroon, and his influence at federal level declined in the following years (the post of Federal Vice-President passed to S. T. Muna in 1970). The KNDP lost its position as a separate party.
- **Disappearance of multi-party politics.** The KNDP, the CPNC and the other parties merged into the Cameroon National Union (CNU) in 1966, creating a single party. This ended political competition in West Cameroon and removed the organised opposition which could have defended its autonomy.
- **Greater federal control over West Cameroon.** Because the Anglophone leaders were divided, Ahidjo gained more influence over West Cameroon through the single party, through appointments and through the federal inspectors of administration. In practice the autonomy of the state was reduced and its government became more and more subordinate to Yaounde. Changes of Prime Minister (Jua in 1965, Muna in 1968) took place with the approval of the federal President.
- **It prepared the end of the federation.** Divided and weakened West Cameroon leaders were not able to resist the centralising policy, and in 1972 the federal system was abolished by a referendum and replaced by a unitary state, which ended the separate existence of West Cameroon.
- **Social and economic effects.** The divisions and the loss of autonomy reduced the government's ability to manage the economy (agriculture, plantations, roads, the development of the Southwest and the Northwest) and encouraged the feeling among Anglophones that their region was neglected, which fed later Anglophone grievances.

**Conclusion.** The KNDP crisis was caused by rivalry between leaders, disagreements about the party's policy and structure, and the pressure of a President who wished to create a single party. It weakened the government of West Cameroon, ended the KNDP as an independent force, removed party competition and strengthened the federal executive, thus helping to bring about the loss of West Cameroon's autonomy and the end of the federal system in 1972.
